dialog.body: Zoning and Inspections, this is Greg.
Hi, good afternoon. Um, my name is Carmen Morales. I'm calling about a fence. I want to put up a fence, and I don't know who I'm supposed to ask.
You got the right place. What are you looking to do?

So, the back of my yard, along the back property line. I want a six-foot fence there. Six feet. Black aluminum, that's the kind I like, the black. Or whatever is allowed tall, you know? If six isn't allowed then whatever the tallest is.
Okay. Black aluminum along the back line. Is this a regular residential lot?
Yes, a house. I'm the homeowner. Just a regular yard, nothing big.
Good. So what's your main question?

My question is, do I need a permit? For a fence. Because my neighbor said no, you only need a permit for a pool fence, and then my sister-in-law said yes, everything needs a permit. So now I have two answers and neither one is the city.

Right, well, I'll give you the city. In general, yes, a fence usually needs a permit here. Height matters, and so does where it goes. A six-foot fence in a back yard is something you'd want to run through us before anybody digs a post hole.
Oh. So the neighbor was wrong. But what about the pool thing? I don't have a pool.
Pools have their own barrier rules on top of it. No pool, so that's not your issue. Your issue is the fence itself needs the permit.
Okay. Okay. So the permit, it's for the fence, not the pool. Got it. Wait, is it for the height only? Like if I did a four-foot fence, no permit?
I wouldn't go planning around that. Even shorter fences can need one. Easiest thing is assume you need it and apply.
Alright. And then, how close can the fence be to the property line? Like, can it go right on the line? Or do I have to go in a few feet? I don't want a fight with the back neighbor.

That's a good thing to ask first. Typically there's a setback, and a lot of people set a fence a bit inside their own line so it's clearly on their property. The exact distance depends on your lot and the zone. When you apply, you'll show where the line is and where the fence sits, and we check it against the rules.
So there's a number, but you don't have the number.

There may be one, depending on your zone, and I'd need your address to look up the zone. I understand you'd rather not give it, that's fine. You can call back with it, or come to the counter and we'll pull it up.
Hmm. I can do that. But what do I bring? A drawing? I'm not an architect.

You don't need to be. A simple sketch of your lot is fine. Show the house, the property lines, and a line for the fence with the length and height. If you have a survey of your property, bring it. That helps a lot with the line question.
A survey. Is that the, the plot plan from when I bought the house? There's a paper in the folder with the little drawing of the house.
That could be it. If it shows the lot lines and measurements, bring it in. If it's a mortgage inspection sketch, it may not be accurate enough, but bring it anyway and we'll look.
Okay, I'll look for the folder. I do my paperwork at the coffee shop on Spring Street, so, the folder is probably in my bag there. Or at home. One of those.
Well, hopefully it's in the bag. Also, you'll want to write down the fence material and the style, so black aluminum, picket style or whatever you pick.
Picket, yes. The flat top. Not the pointy ones.
Fine, put that down. And the height. Say six feet, and if that's more than allowed, we'll tell you at review.
So I ask for six and you tell me if it's too much.
Right. Better than guessing low and wishing you'd asked for more.
Okay. And does the permit take long? Because the contractor wants a date.
I can't give you a firm turnaround on the phone. It depends on how busy we are and whether the application is complete. Complete paperwork moves faster, that much I can tell you.
Complete paperwork. Okay. So, sketch, survey, material, height. Anything else?
Your contact info and the contractor's, if there's one. Can be on the form. You can pick up the form at the counter, or ask for it when you come in.
Can I get the form without the address thing? Like I come in and just, you give me the form?
Sure, anybody can pick up a form. You'll need the address when you fill it out, of course. That's how we find your zone.
Of course, yes. I thought, because I said the fence, you'd say the fence permit is the building permit, or the zoning permit. Which one is it? There's two?
Good question. For a fence, zoning looks at where it goes and how tall, and that's us. Start with us at the counter, and if something else is needed, we'll point you to it.
So it's you, zoning. Not building.
Start with us, yes. We're in the same office area anyway.
Alright. I'm still a little, um, mixed up on the line part. If I put it a little inside, is that always okay?
Inside your own line is usually the safer way, but I can't say a specific distance without the zone. Bring the survey, we'll go over it with you.
Okay. Okay. Thank you, Greg. That helps. I'll find the folder and come in.
Sounds good. Have a good afternoon.
You too. Bye.
